title: Variables and types
bridge: C++ declares a type for every variable, like Java and C#: `int kg = 40; double price = 55.5; bool sold = false; char grade = 'A'; std::string crop = "maize";`. `auto` lets the compiler work it out. Watch out: `7 / 2` is `3` (whole numbers), `7.0 / 2` is `3.5`.
lesson:
Every variable in C++ has a **type** that never changes:

```
int harvestKg = 40;          // whole numbers
double pricePerKg = 55.5;    // decimals
bool sold = false;           // true / false
char grade = 'A';            // one character, single quotes
std::string crop = "maize";  // text (needs #include <string>)
const double Rate = 130.0;   // can't be changed later
auto count = 3;              // compiler works out: int
```

**The integer division trap.** When both sides are `int`, C++ does whole-number division and throws away the rest:

```
int total = 7, count = 2;
double a = total / count;            // 3   (the .5 was lost BEFORE storing)
double b = (double)total / count;    // 3.5 (convert first)
double c = static_cast<double>(total) / count;  // 3.5, the modern way to write it
```

`%` gives the remainder: `7 % 2` is `1`.

Variables that are never given a value hold **garbage** in C++ (whatever was in that memory). Always initialise them. This is one of the classic C++ bugs.

exercises.title: Total weight
exercises.prompt: Write int totalKg(int bags, int kgPerBag) that returns the total weight.

exercises.title: Average without losing the half
exercises.prompt: Write double average(int total, int count) that returns the exact average, e.g. average(7, 2) is 3.5.

tests.hint_if_fail: 7 / 2 with two ints is 3. Convert one side to double first.

hints: Both are int, so / throws away the .5.

quiz.q: What is 7 / 2 in C++ when both are int?
What's in int x; before you set it?
quiz.why: Uninitialised locals hold leftover memory. Always initialise.
char holds one character; std::string holds text.
